passages.text: Targeted Next-Generation Sequencing in the Diagnosis of Facial Dysostoses
Background

Defects in the development of the first and second pharyngeal arches and their derivatives result in abnormal formation of the craniofacial complex, consequently giving rise to facial dysostoses (FDs). <sentence_start/>FDs represent a group of rare and highly heterogeneous disease entities that encompass mandibulofacial dysostoses (MFDs) with normal extremities and acrofacial dysostoses (AFDs) with limb anomalies in addition to craniofacial defects.
Methods

We examined 11 families with variable clinical symptoms of FDs, in most of which only one member was affected. <sentence_start/>We applied two custom gene panels-first comprising 37 genes related to the genetic disorders of craniofacial development such as FDs (On-Demand AmpliSeq Thermo Fisher Scientific gene panel with two primer pools) and second composed of 61 genes and 11 single nucleotide variants (SNVs) known to be involved in the development of skull malformations, mainly in the form of craniosynostoses (SureSelect Agilent Technologies). <sentence_start/>Targeted next-generation sequencing (NGS) was performed using the Ion Torrent S5 platform. <sentence_start/>To confirm the presence of each detected variant, we have analyzed a genomic region of interest using Sanger sequencing.
Results

In this paper, we summarized the results of custom targeted gene panel sequencing in the cohort of sixteen patients from 11 consecutive families affected by distinct forms of FDs. <sentence_start/>We have found three novel pathogenic variants in the <italic toggle="yes">TCOF1</italic> gene-c.2145_2148dupAAAG p.(Ser717Lys<italic toggle="yes">fs</italic><sup>∗</sup>42), c.4370delA p.(Lys1457Arg<italic toggle="yes">fs</italic><sup>∗</sup>118), c.83G>C p.(Arg28Pro) causing Treacher Collins syndrome type 1, two novel missense variants in the <italic toggle="yes">EFTUD2</italic> gene-c.491A>G p.(Asp164Gly) and c.779T>A p.(Ile260Asn) in two female patients affected by acrofacial dysostosis Guion-Almeida type, one previously reported-c.403C>T (p.Arg135Cys), as well as one novel missense variant-c.128C>T p.(Pro43Leu) in the <italic toggle="yes">DHODH</italic> gene in the male patient with Miller syndrome and finally one known pathogenic variant c.574G>T p.(Glu192<sup>∗</sup>) in the <italic toggle="yes">SF3B4</italic> gene in the patient with Nager syndrome.
Conclusion

Our study confirms the efficiency and clinical utility of the targeted gene panel sequencing and shows that this strategy is suitable and efficient in the molecular screening of variable forms of FDs.
Background

The human skull composes of neuro- and viscerocranium that both develop independently from one another. <sentence_start/>Neurocranium mainly forms from the first five somites and the unsegmented somitomeres rostral to the first somite, whereas, viscerocranium, namely facial skeleton, forms from pharyngeal arches (<citation rid="B16" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.3340/jkns.2016.59.3.192" pmid="27226848" pmcid="PMC4877539" count="1">Jin et al., 2016</citation>).

Defects concerning embryonic development of the first and second pharyngeal arches and their derivatives result in facial dysostoses (FDs), which encompass a group of rare and extremely variable clinical disease entities. <sentence_start/>FDs have been subdivided into mandibulofacial dysostoses (MFDs) with normal extremities and acrofacial dysostoses (AFDs) with limb anomalies in addition to craniofacial malformations (Table 1; <citation rid="B31" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1002/ajmg.c.31375" pmid="24123981" pmcid="PMC3870197" count="1">Trainor and Andrews, 2013</citation>; <citation rid="B35" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1111/cge.12123" pmid="23565775" count="1">Wieczorek, 2013</citation>). <sentence_start/>The characteristic facial features of FDs involve hypoplasia of the maxilla, mandible, zygomatic arches, various anomalies of the external and middle ear, and other facial defects including coloboma of the lower eyelid with partial to total absence of eyelashes or dysmorphic features, such as down-slanting palpebral fissures. <sentence_start/>Limb defects represent a broad spectrum of post- or preaxial abnormalities, including polydactyly, oligodactyly, and brachydactyly (<citation rid="B23" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1136/jmg.28.10.695" pmid="1941965" pmcid="PMC1017057" count="1">Ogilvy-Stuart and Parsons, 1991</citation>; <citation rid="B20" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1136/jmg.30.9.779" pmid="8411075" pmcid="PMC1016537" count="1">McDonald and Gorski, 1993</citation>; <citation rid="B36" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1002/ajmg.a.32747" pmid="19334086" count="1">Wieczorek et al., 2009</citation>; <citation rid="B22" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1038/ng.499" pmid="19915526" pmcid="PMC2847889" count="1">Ng et al., 2010</citation>; <citation rid="B27" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1093/hmg/dds218" pmid="22692683" count="1">Rainger et al., 2012</citation>; <citation rid="B7" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1007/s00439-013-1295-2" pmid="23568615" count="1">Czeschik et al., 2013</citation>; <citation rid="B31" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1002/ajmg.c.31375" pmid="24123981" pmcid="PMC3870197" count="1">Trainor and Andrews, 2013</citation>; <citation rid="B35" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1111/cge.12123" pmid="23565775" count="1">Wieczorek, 2013</citation>). <sentence_start/>Additional clinical signs, which may be present comprise microcephaly, cleft palate, oligodontia, defects of the internal organs, short stature, psychomotor delay, and intellectual disability (<citation rid="B15" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1097/01.mcd.0000220603.09661.7e" pmid="16760738" count="1">Guion-Almeida et al., 2006</citation>; <citation rid="B35" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1111/cge.12123" pmid="23565775" count="1">Wieczorek, 2013</citation>).

Importantly, FDs present a high clinical heterogeneity, including a marked inter- and intra-familial variability of their phenotypic expression what in turn frequently impedes reaching an exact clinical diagnosis and its confirmation at a molecular level (<citation rid="B11" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1002/ajmg.a.30010" pmid="15150774" count="1">Dixon et al., 2004</citation>; <citation rid="B33" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1038/gim.2015.29" pmid="25790162" count="1">Vincent et al., 2016</citation>). <sentence_start/>Consequently, many patients affected by FDs remain molecularly undiagnosed and bereft of reliable genetic counseling, prenatal and preimplantation testing, but also of a proper and unequivocal clinical classification (<citation rid="B22" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1038/ng.499" pmid="19915526" pmcid="PMC2847889" count="1">Ng et al., 2010</citation>; <citation rid="B2" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1016/j.ajhg.2012.04.004" pmid="22541558" pmcid="PMC3376638" count="1">Bernier et al., 2012</citation>; <citation rid="B19" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1016/j.ajhg.2011.12.023" pmid="22305528" pmcid="PMC3276671" count="1">Lines et al., 2012</citation>; <citation rid="B12" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1186/s13023-019-1136-z" pmid="31307516" pmcid="PMC6631538" count="1">Fan et al., 2019</citation>).
Materials and Methods

All procedures were performed under the ethical standards of the institutional and national research committee and with the 1964 Helsinki declaration and its later amendments or comparable ethical standards. <sentence_start/>We granted ethics approval from the Institutional Review Board of Poznan University of Medical Sciences (no. 741/17 and 742/17 obtained on 22<sup>nd</sup> June 2017). <sentence_start/>We examined 11 families with variable clinical symptoms of FDs, in most of which only one member was affected. <sentence_start/>We extracted genomic DNA from the peripheral blood lymphocytes using the MagCore HF16 Automated Nucleic Acid Extractor and quantified each gDNA using the Agilent Technologies TapeStation 2200 and Qubit.
Targeted Next-Generation Sequencing
Facial Dysostoses Panel

We designed the custom On-Demand AmpliSeq (Thermo Fisher Scientific) gene panel with two primer pools and performed targeted sequencing of 37 genes related to the genetic disorders of craniofacial development, including FDs (patients 1.4, 1.6, 2-4, 6 and 7; Supplementary Table 1). <sentence_start/>The gene panel was 145.51 kb in size and comprised 761 amplicons, intervals sequenced for each gene were shown in Supplementary Table 2. <sentence_start/>The barcoded genomic DNA libraries were constructed according to the ‘manufacturer’s sample preparation protocol (Ion AmpliSeq Library Kit 2.0; On-Demand Panels). <sentence_start/>Pooled libraries were subjected to emulsion PCR on Ion Chef<sup>TM</sup> instrument using the Ion 520<sup>TM</sup> and 530<sup>TM</sup>Kit, according to the standard protocol and sequenced on the Ion Torrent S5 platform.
Craniosynostosis Panel

The custom SureSelect (Agilent Technologies) gene panel comprised of 61 genes and 11 SNVs known to be involved in the development of craniofacial malformations, particularly craniosynostosis (CS), was designed (Supplementary Table 3). <sentence_start/>Intervals sequenced for each gene were shown in Supplementary Table 4. <sentence_start/>Targeted sequencing, encompassing 225.709 kb was performed for patient 5. <sentence_start/>We prepared the NGS library using hybridized capture-based target enrichment approach and sequenced it on the Ion Torrent S5 platform (<citation rid="B5" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1038/s41598-020-61048-5" pmid="32139749" pmcid="PMC7058001" count="1">Bukowska-Olech et al., 2020</citation>).
Next-Generation Sequencing Data Analysis

The present analysis follows the approach previously described in <citation rid="B5" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1038/s41598-020-61048-5" pmid="32139749" pmcid="PMC7058001" count="1">Bukowska-Olech et al. (2020)</citation>. <sentence_start/>Briefly, the reads were cleaned and aligned to GrCh37 human reference sequence using the TorrentBrowser 5.0.4 software (Thermo Fisher Scientific). <sentence_start/>The alignments were further processed using IonReporter 5.2 pipeline (Thermo Fisher Scientific), which incorporated variant calling with Torrent Variant Caller 5.4-11. <sentence_start/>Each variant was examined based on four criteria (read depth− ≥ 20, strandedness− ≤ 4:1, PHRED score ≥ 30 and variant frequency ≥ 0.15). <sentence_start/>The coverage of individual genes and exons was performed using bedtools 2.27.1 (<italic toggle="yes">coverage</italic> subcommand) against panel-specific BED files defining coding parts of canonical transcripts for each constituent gene (RefSeq mapped on UCSC hg19 reference; 5 bp padding around each exon included; Supplementary Tables 5-8).

Previous clinical annotation of called variants was obtained from Human Gene Mutation Database (HGMD) Professional (accessed on 14/02/2019), ClinVar (accessed on 27/07/2019) and dbSNP (accessed on 27/07/2019). <sentence_start/>The predictions for SIFT, PolyPhen, and PhyloP (46-way) tools were retrieved from IonReporter result files. <sentence_start/>Population allele frequencies were annotated by Ensembl/Variant Effect Predictor (software version 94, database version 94); additionally, gnomAD database was queried for homozygosity/heterozygosity of individual variants (version 2.1.1 of both exome and genome subsets; accessed on 27/07/2019 using tabix 1.5 software). <sentence_start/>The scores for Combined Annotation Dependent Depletion were obtained from CADD webserver (v1.4, accessed on 27/07/2019). <sentence_start/>MutationTaster results were obtained using the “query chromosomal position” option of the public webserver (accessed on 27/07/2019).
Sanger Sequencing

To confirm the presence of each pathogenic or likely pathogenic variant, as well as of variant of uncertain significance (VUS), we have analyzed the genomic region of interest using Sanger sequencing. <sentence_start/>The online available Primer3 tool was used to design specific primers for the amplification. <sentence_start/>The PCR reactions and PCR products purification were carried out following standard protocols. <sentence_start/>Sanger sequencing was performed using dye-terminator chemistry (kit v.3, ABI 3130XL) and run on automated sequencer Applied Biosystems Prism 3700 DNA Analyzer. <sentence_start/>Variants were annotated against the reference sequences: <italic toggle="yes">DHODH</italic>- , , , ; <italic toggle="yes">EFTUD2</italic>- , , , ; <italic toggle="yes">SF3B4</italic>- , , , <italic toggle="yes">TCOF1</italic>- , , , following the Human Genome Variation Society (HGVS) nomenclature guidelines (<citation rid="B9" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1002/humu.22981" pmid="26931183" count="1">den Dunnen et al., 2016</citation>; Table 2).
Results
Clinical Assessment

We recruited 11 consecutive families in whom 16 individuals were affected by various forms of FDs. <sentence_start/>Four families (no. 1-3, 6) received the clinical diagnosis of MFDs defined as hypoplastic maxilla, mandible, and zygomatic arches with down-slanting palpebral fissures. <sentence_start/>Six families (no. 4, 8-11) were clinically diagnosed with AFDs since the affected individuals showed not only craniofacial but also limb involvement. <sentence_start/>In one family (family 5), we did not recognize FD based on the dysmorphological assessment. <sentence_start/>The detailed clinical data of all screened patients is set forth in Supplementary Data Sheet 1.
Genetic Analyses

Targeted NGS allowed us to reach an exact diagnosis of FDs in seven out of eleven families (no. 1-7). <sentence_start/>Among them, we identified six novel and two previously reported variants in the following genes-<italic toggle="yes">TCOF1</italic>, <italic toggle="yes">SF3B4</italic>, <italic toggle="yes">EFTUD2</italic>, and <italic toggle="yes">DHODH</italic> (Table 2). <sentence_start/>The mean coverage for FDs panel ranged from 214 to 430 reads per gene, whereas for CS panel from 272 to 488 reads per gene (Supplementary Tables 5, 7).

In families no 1-3, we found three novel heterozygous variants in the <italic toggle="yes">TCOF1</italic> that gave rise to the most well-characterized MFD, i.e., Treacher Collins syndrome (TCS) type 1 (TCS1, MIM:154500). <sentence_start/>The major clinical features of all affected individuals were summarized in Table 3. <sentence_start/>The rest of the diagnosed patients was affected by different types of AFDs. <sentence_start/>In a sporadic female case from family no 4, we identified the heterozygous variant in the <italic toggle="yes">SF3B4</italic> gene causing Nager syndrome (MIM:54400). <sentence_start/>Two other sporadic female cases from families no 5 and 6 harbored <italic toggle="yes">de novo</italic> heterozygous variants within the <italic toggle="yes">EFTUD2</italic> gene and presented with variable symptoms of acrofacial dysostosis Guion-Almeida type (AFDGA, MIM:610536). <sentence_start/>The comparison of their clinical features was shown in Table 4. <sentence_start/>Finally, in a male proband from family no 7, we diagnosed Miller syndrome (MIM:263750), as we found two biallelic variants in the <italic toggle="yes">DHODH</italic> gene. <sentence_start/>Importantly, none of the detected alterations was present in gnomAD or ExAC databases or found in 200 ethnically matched control alleles from our in-house, population-specific database. <sentence_start/>Segregation analysis of the causative variants performed in families 1-6 was consistent with the expected autosomal dominant inheritance pattern (Figures 2, 3C,F, 4C, 5D,H), whereas in family 7 with autosomal recessive pattern (Figure 6E). <sentence_start/>The results of molecular screening and segregation analyses were shown in Figures 1-6 and Supplementary Figures 1A-I.

Discussion

Before the advent of NGS, identification of the underlying causative genetic lesions in individuals affected by molecularly complex genetic syndromes such as FDs was often difficult or sometimes impossible (<citation rid="B12" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1186/s13023-019-1136-z" pmid="31307516" pmcid="PMC6631538" count="1">Fan et al., 2019</citation>). <sentence_start/>In an excellent review on human facial dysostoses, Wieczorek emphasized that the current classification of FDs bases mostly on the clinical characteristics of the facial features as well as the presence or absence of additional symptoms (Table 1; <citation rid="B35" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1111/cge.12123" pmid="23565775" count="1">Wieczorek, 2013</citation>). <sentence_start/>The molecular confirmation of FDs is unquestionably crucial not only for reliable genetic counseling, prenatal and preimplantation testing, but also for a proper and unequivocal clinical classification.

In this paper, we summarized the results of the custom targeted gene panel sequencing in a group of 16 patients from 11 consecutive families affected by distinct forms of FDs that were consulted in our genetic clinic. <sentence_start/>In this cohort, we detected three novel heterozygous variants within the <italic toggle="yes">TCOF1</italic> gene, two of which were frameshifts: c.2145_2148dupAAAG p.(Ser717Lys<italic toggle="yes">fs</italic><sup>∗</sup>42) (family 1; Figure 2), c.4370delA p.(Lys1457Arg<italic toggle="yes">fs</italic><sup>∗</sup>118) (family 3; Figure 3F), while one was a missense alteration c.83G>C p.(Arg28Pro) (family 2; Figure 3C). <sentence_start/><italic toggle="yes">In silico</italic> analyses predicted that frameshifts truncating Treacle protein at codons 717 and 1457 were pathogenic, whereas a missense variant p.(Arg28Pro) was initially classified as a VUS (Table 2). <sentence_start/>The results of segregation analysis performed in family 2 showed that the variant occurred <italic toggle="yes">de novo</italic>, suggesting its contribution to the patient’s phenotype (Figure 3C). <sentence_start/>The rest of the diagnosed individuals was affected by various types of AFDs. <sentence_start/>Among them, we identified one previously reported nonsense heterozygous pathogenic variant in the <italic toggle="yes">SF3B4</italic> gene-c.574G>T p.(Glu192<sup>∗</sup>) (family 4; Figure 4C), two novel missense likely pathogenic heterozygous variants in the <italic toggle="yes">EFTUD2</italic> gene, which occurred <italic toggle="yes">de novo</italic>-c.491A>G p.(Asp164Gly) (family 5; Figure 5D), c.779T>A p.(Ile260Asn) (family 6; Figure 5H), and one previously reported-c.403C>T (p.Arg135Cys) (evaluated as pathogenic), as well as one novel-c.128C>T p.(Pro43Leu) missense variants (evaluated as VUS), both located in trans orientation in the <italic toggle="yes">DHODH</italic> gene (family 7; Figure 6E).

Pathogenic variants in the <italic toggle="yes">TCOF1</italic> but also the <italic toggle="yes">POLR1D</italic> and <italic toggle="yes">POLR1C</italic> genes have been previously associated with Treacher Collins syndrome (TCS) types 1-3, respectively (<citation rid="B10" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1038/ng0296-130" pmid="8563749" count="1">Dixon et al., 1996</citation>; <citation rid="B8" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1038/ng.724" pmid="21131976" count="1">Dauwerse et al., 2011</citation>; <citation rid="B28" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1038/gim.2014.12" pmid="24603435" count="1">Schaefer et al., 2014</citation>). <sentence_start/>According to the current review of medical literature, in the majority of patients (i.e., 77-89%) causative alterations are found within the <italic toggle="yes">TCOF1</italic> gene (encoding Treacle protein). <sentence_start/>Consistently with these results, we detected all three causative variants in the <italic toggle="yes">TCOF1</italic> (families no 1-3), and not in other TCS-related genes (<citation rid="B8" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1038/ng.724" pmid="21131976" count="1">Dauwerse et al., 2011</citation>). <sentence_start/>TCS is characterized by malar hypoplasia, micrognathia, down-slanting palpebral fissures, atresia of the external auditory canals, anomalies of the middle ear ossicles, and bilateral conductive hearing loss (<citation rid="B30" ref-type="bibr" pmid="13835025" doi="10.1148/74.2.225" count="1">Stovin et al., 1960</citation>; <citation rid="B25" ref-type="bibr" pmid="7273449" doi="10.1111/j.1365-2273.1981.tb01782.x" count="1">Phelps et al., 1981</citation>; <citation rid="B32" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1038/ejhg.2008.221" pmid="19107148" pmcid="PMC2986179" count="1">Trainor et al., 2009</citation>; <citation rid="B33" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1038/gim.2015.29" pmid="25790162" count="1">Vincent et al., 2016</citation>). <sentence_start/>Nevertheless, the phenotype often varies not only between, but also within the affected families. <sentence_start/>We have confirmed that in cases with TCS1 there is no clear genotype-phenotype correlation and that the expressivity of the clinical symptoms shows considerable intra- and interfamilial variability suggesting the influence of additional contributors (Table 3). <sentence_start/>However, the presence of modifying factors, probably involved in the process of mRNA level regulation, requires further research.

In the vast majority of families affected by AFDs, we have suspected Nager syndrome, which surprisingly was proved genetically only in one individual (patient 4). <sentence_start/>The families 5 and 7 that were misdiagnosed with Nager syndrome turned out to represent AFDGA (family 6) and Miller syndrome (family 7). <sentence_start/>Nager syndrome, along with AFDGA and Miller syndrome, share similar facial and skeletal features, hence the unambiguous diagnosis based only on the clinical symptoms may be uncertain (<citation rid="B31" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1002/ajmg.c.31375" pmid="24123981" pmcid="PMC3870197" count="1">Trainor and Andrews, 2013</citation>; <citation rid="B35" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1111/cge.12123" pmid="23565775" count="1">Wieczorek, 2013</citation>). <sentence_start/>Variants in the <italic toggle="yes">SF3B4</italic> gene that encodes a splicing factor 3B subunit 4 are found in about half of the patients clinically diagnosed with Nager syndrome (<citation rid="B2" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1016/j.ajhg.2012.04.004" pmid="22541558" pmcid="PMC3376638" count="1">Bernier et al., 2012</citation>; <citation rid="B7" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1007/s00439-013-1295-2" pmid="23568615" count="1">Czeschik et al., 2013</citation>). <sentence_start/>The main phenotypic features of this condition involve facial characteristics similar to TCS and preaxial limb defects such as hypoplasia or aplasia of the radius and thumbs, radioulnar synostosis or triphalangeal thumbs (<citation rid="B4" ref-type="bibr" pmid="4469973" count="1">Bowen and Harley, 1974</citation>; <citation rid="B21" ref-type="bibr" pmid="401476" count="1">Meyerson et al., 1977</citation>; <citation rid="B24" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1002/ajmg.1320270425" pmid="3425605" count="1">Opitz, 1987</citation>; <citation rid="B20" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1136/jmg.30.9.779" pmid="8411075" pmcid="PMC1016537" count="1">McDonald and Gorski, 1993</citation>; <citation rid="B35" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1111/cge.12123" pmid="23565775" count="1">Wieczorek, 2013</citation>). <sentence_start/>A nonsense alteration p.(Glu192<sup>∗</sup>) within splicing factor 3B subunit 4, which occurred in patient 4, was firstly described by Czeschik et al. in a female patient with Nager syndrome, who manifested very similar symptoms to patient 4. <sentence_start/>Both individuals presented with extreme hypoplasia of the mandible, micrognathia, hypoplastic thumbs, bilateral limited elbow extension, hearing loss and delayed psychomotor development, with absent speech due to severe hypoplasia of the mandibulofacial structures (<citation rid="B7" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1007/s00439-013-1295-2" pmid="23568615" count="1">Czeschik et al., 2013</citation>). <sentence_start/>Additionally, patient 4 had an ectopic left kidney, which was located in the pelvis.

In families no. 5 and 6, we have found novel heterozygous variants in <italic toggle="yes">EFTUD2</italic>, the gene encoding elongation factor Tu GTP binding domain containing 2, resulting in AFDGA (<citation rid="B15" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1097/01.mcd.0000220603.09661.7e" pmid="16760738" count="1">Guion-Almeida et al., 2006</citation>; <citation rid="B19" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1016/j.ajhg.2011.12.023" pmid="22305528" pmcid="PMC3276671" count="1">Lines et al., 2012</citation>). <sentence_start/>This entity was initially classified as mandibulofacial dysostosis Guion-Almeida type (MFDGA). <sentence_start/>Nevertheless, due to the occurrence of limb anomalies in some patients, it was reclassified to AFDs (<citation rid="B34" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1186/1750-1172-8-110" pmid="23879989" pmcid="PMC3727992" count="1">Voigt et al., 2013</citation>). <sentence_start/>The clinical spectrum of AFDGA is broad and consists of microcephaly, postnatal-onset growth deficiency, choanal atresia, heart and gastrointestinal anomalies, preaxial polydactyly, slender fingers, and proximally placed thumbs (<citation rid="B15" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1097/01.mcd.0000220603.09661.7e" pmid="16760738" count="1">Guion-Almeida et al., 2006</citation>; <citation rid="B37" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1002/ajmg.a.31752" pmid="17497718" count="1">Wieczorek et al., 2007</citation>, <citation rid="B36" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1002/ajmg.a.32747" pmid="19334086" count="1">2009</citation>; <citation rid="B19" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1016/j.ajhg.2011.12.023" pmid="22305528" pmcid="PMC3276671" count="1">Lines et al., 2012</citation>; <citation rid="B14" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1016/j.ajhg.2015.01.015" pmid="25772936" pmcid="PMC4385188" count="1">Gordon et al., 2015</citation>). <sentence_start/>Very recently, new craniofacial phenotypes, i.e., metopic craniosynostosis (CS) and cleft lip and palate, were reported in two individuals carrying heterozygous variants-c.2466+1G>A in intron 24 and c.2333C>A in exon 23 of <italic toggle="yes">EFTUD2</italic>. <sentence_start/>These cases were initially suspected of having an alternative craniofacial syndrome and were eventually diagnosed with MFDGA (<citation rid="B18" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1177/1055665618806379" pmid="30343593" count="1">Lacour et al., 2019</citation>). <sentence_start/>Similarly, patient 5 also presented with very unusual craniofacial features, including metopic synostosis and high forehead that were not suggestive for AFDGA.

Finally, in patient 7, we described compound heterozygous variants in <italic toggle="yes">DHODH</italic> gene. <sentence_start/>Biallelic variants in <italic toggle="yes">DHODH</italic> gene result in defects in pyrimidine biogenesis and give rise to Miller syndrome that has an autosomal recessive inheritance. <sentence_start/>Limb anomalies include postaxial abnormalities, such as the absence of fifth digits with or without shortening and deviation of forearms with ulnar and radial hypoplasia, and syndactyly (<citation rid="B13" ref-type="bibr" pmid="5808539" count="1">Genee, 1969</citation>; <citation rid="B23" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1136/jmg.28.10.695" pmid="1941965" pmcid="PMC1017057" count="1">Ogilvy-Stuart and Parsons, 1991</citation>; <citation rid="B6" ref-type="bibr" pmid="8357564" count="1">Chrzanowska and Fryns, 1993</citation>; <citation rid="B22" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1038/ng.499" pmid="19915526" pmcid="PMC2847889" count="1">Ng et al., 2010</citation>). <sentence_start/>The first pathogenic missense variant (p.Arg135Cys) has been reported previously in six individuals affected by Miller syndrome who were compound heterozygous for (p.Arg135Cys) in combination with one of the following alterations-c.155A>G (p.Glu52Gly), c.1036C>T (p.Arg346Trp), and c.1175A>G (p.Asp392Gly). <sentence_start/>All those patients, including patient 7 (Figures 6A-D), presented with strikingly similar features, encompassing severe micrognathia, cleft lip and/or palate, as well as hypoplasia or aplasia of the postaxial rays of the limbs (<citation rid="B22" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1038/ng.499" pmid="19915526" pmcid="PMC2847889" count="1">Ng et al., 2010</citation>; <citation rid="B1" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1097/MCD.0b013e3283416701" pmid="21346561" count="1">Al Kaissi et al., 2011</citation>; <citation rid="B27" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1093/hmg/dds218" pmid="22692683" count="1">Rainger et al., 2012</citation>). <sentence_start/>The second missense variant c.128C>T p.(Pro43Leu) identified by us was novel.

The diagnostic success rate of the presented approach achieved 64%. <sentence_start/>Undiagnosed cases (families 8-11) may harbor other types of causative alterations that cannot be detected by targeted NGS, such as deep intronic or regulatory mutations affecting genes included in custom gene panels. <sentence_start/>Alternatively, causative mutations may be located elsewhere in the genome and not in the genes known to be involved in the pathogenesis of FDs. <sentence_start/>Therefore, in cases without the exact genetic diagnosis, another type of molecular investigation, including whole-genome sequencing (WGS) should be considered. <sentence_start/>Indeed, the introduction of WGS in the molecular diagnostics of FDs requires advanced <italic toggle="yes">in silico</italic> and functional analyses, which are both necessary for the interpretation and proving of pathogenicity of genomic alterations (<citation rid="B29" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1016/j.ajhg.2016.07.005" pmid="27569544" pmcid="PMC5011059" count="1">Smedley et al., 2016</citation>; <citation rid="B3" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1186/s13059-018-1546-6" pmid="30359302" pmcid="PMC6203199" count="1">Bodea et al., 2018</citation>; <citation rid="B26" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1186/s13023-019-1127-0" pmid="31234920" pmcid="PMC6591893" count="1">Posey, 2019</citation>). <sentence_start/>The proportion of molecularly undiagnosed patients, however, clearly suggests that some of the genetic lesions, causative for FDs, lie within non-coding DNA, and could be picked up only by WGS (<citation rid="B17" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1002/dvg.23271" pmid="30548771" pmcid="PMC6503678" count="1">Kindberg and Bush, 2019</citation>).

In conclusion, with this report, we demonstrated the clinical utility of NGS targeted gene panel approach as a valuable and cost-effective first-tier testing in the molecular analysis of patients presenting with FDs. <sentence_start/>We described the clinical phenotypes of seven families showing distinct forms of FDs and identified six novel and two previously described pathogenic variants. <sentence_start/>Consequently, we highlighted the need for molecular confirmation of FDs, which is crucial for a reliable genetic counseling, an early prenatal and preimplantation testing, but also a proper and unequivocal clinical classification.
